title: wavepacket-surge-benchmark-diary-daniel
content:
Context and goal:
- Quick personal log of a run I did to understand tail behavior for 'wavepacket' arrival shapes (sine-modulated Poisson) against the 8xA100 serving pool. Trying to capture repeatable steps + raw observations so we can iterate.

Hypothesis:
- Periodic microbursts (wavepackets) with short high-density windows overwhelm batching heuristic and cause >2x p99 inflations vs steady Poisson at same average QPS.
- Root levers: batch timeout, max-batch-size, KV cache warm/priming strategy, preemption/backpressure thresholds.

Setup summary:
- Model: openlm-7b-quant (seq_len=1024) pinned to instance group rwd-dedicated-8xA100-32G
- Runtime: rwd-serving v3.8.1 (local build with debug batch-allocator flag enabled)
- Load generator: custom tool 'wavegen-v0.4' (node) that emits sine-modulated Poisson arrivals: lambda(t) = base + amp * sin(2*pi*t/period).
- Test parameters: base=60 qps, amp=90 qps, period=30s (i.e., bursts lasting ~8-10s), test duration 30 min.
- Payload: avg tokens 128 (prompt+gen), temperature=0.2, streaming disabled.
- Concurrency settings: 200 client connections, 4 clients across 4 worker hosts.
- Batch config under test: default (batch_timeout_ms=15, max_batch_tokens=16384, max_batch_examples=32) and tuned (batch_timeout_ms=6, max_batch_examples=16).

Commands (approx):
- Start runtime: ./rwd-serving --config configs/dedicated-8xA100.json --enable-debug-batch-allocator
- Launch wavegen: node wavegen.js --base 60 --amp 90 --period 30 --duration 1800 --conns 200 --seq 1024 --token-dist "128,32" --targets http://rwd-host:8080/generate

Key raw metrics (representative run, default batch config):
- avg QPS (observed): 145
- throughput (tokens/sec): ~18k
- p50 latency (response complete): 48 ms
- p95 latency: 210 ms
- p99 latency: 1.12 s
- p999 latency: 2.8 s (tail spikes during burst onset)
- batch size median: 22 examples; during peaks median -> 28, spikes hit 32 (capped)
- KV cache hit-rate: 0.82 overall; drops to 0.74 during burst start (cache priming gap)
- observed CPU on host: 78% avg, GPU utilization: 91% during bursts
- observed queue length (server-side): short spikes to 110 reqs queued at burst onset, then drained within 1.5-3s once batching ramps.

Tuned run (batch_timeout_ms=6, max_batch_examples=16):
- avg QPS: 143 (similar)
- p50: 46 ms
- p95: 160 ms (improved)
- p99: 520 ms (improved ~2x)
- p999: 1.4 s
- batch size median: 12; during peaks -> 16 (capped)
- queue spikes smaller: to ~48 reqs queued
- noticed throughput drop during sustained peak slices if we over-aggressively reduce batch window (net tokens/sec lost ~8%)

Short conclusions / takeaways:
- Reducing batch_timeout and max_examples helps considerably for tail latency (p99/p999) at the expense of peak token throughput. For latency-sensitive customers, the tradeoff looks attractive up to a ~8% cost in tokens/sec.
- The biggest jerk in tail happens at burst onsets where KV-cache effective hit-rate dips (priming IO + model kv-population mismatch). Those ~1-3s tails correlate with cache-miss floods.
- Batching heuristics that adapt to arrival curvature (d/dt of QPS) would likely reduce onset spikes: i.e., shorten timeout proactively when a fast up-slope is detected.

Observations / oddities to investigate:
- Occasionally saw a 6-8s outlier (~p9999) where request stayed in queue but server reported 'batch allocated' and then timed out. Need to check RPC layer and any per-batch backoff/retry interactions. Create trace id next time.
- The debug batch allocator logs show occasional lock contention inside allocator when two large batches try to merge; need to repro with smaller cluster and instrumentation.
- When I re-ran with streaming enabled, p99 improved slightly (less variance on response complete) but overall complexity increased (client-side windowing). Worth a separate pass.

Next actions / TODOs:
- [ ] Re-run with KV-cache priming baseline: run short warmup traffic 30s before every burst window, measure difference.
- [ ] Add instrumentation: emit trace-id from wavegen and ensure server logs batch_id -> trace_id mapping; upload to GH PR linked above.
- [ ] Try adaptive batch timeout: simple PID-like controller that drops batch_timeout by 2x for 3s when slope > threshold. Quick simulator in Python first.
- [ ] Investigate lock contention in allocator: reproduce with stress harness and enable lock profiling (tsan-like).
- [ ] Run with heterogenous GPU mix (mix of A100 + H100) to see scheduling artifacts.

Notes to self / quick heuristics:
- If p99 > 3x desired SLO during 10s burst windows, try batch_timeout<=8ms and max_examples<=16 as first cut.
- If tokens/sec drop >10% after tuning, consider adding short burst-only burst-queue lane with temporary reserved slots (costly but stabilizes p99).

References and context links:
- Linear: WV-421 (wavepacket load generator)
- Bench PR: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pull/312 (contains the wavegen code and parse scripts)
- Slack thread: #eng-runtime 'wavepacket burst observations' dated Feb 20 2026

Freeform scratch / raw CLI outputs (pasted):
- default run snippet: "[2026-02-20 14:08:32] avg_qps=145 p50=48ms p95=210ms p99=1120ms queued_peak=110 batch_median=22"
- tuned run snippet: "[2026-02-20 15:42:18] avg_qps=143 p50=46ms p95=160ms p99=520ms queued_peak=48 batch_median=12"

Random thoughts:
- Could try a middle ground: keep batch_timeout small for first 150ms of a detected up-slope, then relax to normal to recover throughput. Might need two-tier timers per worker.
- Consider exposing an 'arrival-curvature' metric in console so customers can correlate time windows with SLO breaches.

End of log. Will re-run after adding trace-id mapping and capture full flamegraphs for allocator.
